Highlight

FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Recognize the importance of early and appropriate antibiotic coverage for open fractures.
Characterize open fractures and appropriately use the Gustilo-Anderson classification system.
Explain how to perform a thorough débridement.
Review controversies of negative pressure wound therapy and other adjunctive treatment
options to optimize outcomes of open fractures.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Definition—An open fracture is a soft-tissue injury that includes a fracture. Communication is
present between the fracture site and an overlying break in the skin.





Epidemiology
Approximately 4% of all fractures are open.
In the United States, 250,000 open fractures occur annually.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Open fractures can occur in any region of the body, and the unique osteology of the region
should be noted and understood.
Open fractures create a disruption in skin, muscle, fascia, periosteum, and bone, allowing
contaminants into the fracture environment.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
In-to-out injury: enough force is imparted to the bone to permit fracture fragments to extrude
through the muscle and the underlying tissues and skin
Out-to-in injury: crush injuries or penetrating trauma damage the skin and underlying tissue,
allowing access to the underlying bone
Risk Factors
High-energy trauma
Crush injuries
Blast injuries
Associated Injuries
Surrounding soft tissues should be carefully evaluated, and all nonviable tissue should be
débrided. This may necessitate eventual plastic surgery involvement or flap coverage.
Incidence of vascular and neurologic injury is higher with open fractures, and surgeons should
perform a thorough evaluation on patient presentation.
Injury Classification
Gustilo-Anderson classification system (Table 1)
Table 1 Gustilo-Anderson Classification of Open Fractures

Type
Description
I
 Wound <1 cm in length; minimal contamination and soft-tissue damage; usually
an inside-to-outside injury.
II
 Wound between 1 and 10 cm in length; soft-tissue injury and crushing are
moderate; comminution is minimal.
III
 Severe soft-tissue injury, contamination, and crushing; high-energy injury with
comminution; wound size may be >10 cm.
IIIA
 Adequate soft-tissue coverage after débridement; high-energy trauma
irrespective of the size of the wound.
IIIB

IIIC
 Any open fracture with an arterial injury requiring repair
Reproduced from Stinner DJ: Gunshot wounds and open fractures, in Lieberman JR, ed: AAOS
Comprehensive Orthopaedic Review, ed 3. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020, pp 875-883.

Injury Classification
The Gustilo-Anderson Classification is the most commonly used system for classifying
open fractures. It requires that surgical débridement be performed before assigning a
type. All factors are considered in assigning the type; however, typically, the highest
possible type should be assigned based on each factor.
Orthopaedic Trauma Association Open Fracture Classification (Table 2): The Orthopaedic
Trauma Association Open Fracture Classification also is intended to be applied after
initial débridement. The classification system assigns a severity—mild (1), moderate (2),
or severe (3)—to each of five categories: skin, muscle, arterial, contamination, and bone
loss. This new classification system is associated with moderate to excellent
interobserver reliability and appears to have predictive value for several outcomes,
including amputation and infection requiring the use of intravenous antibiotic agents.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Mechanism of injury
Important for understanding the amount of force and energy imparted
Location of injury
Certain environments, such as marinas and farmyards, require specific antibiotic coverage
given the typical microbiome found in them. The patient history should include the location
of injury to ensure appropriate antibiotic coverage and to anticipate possible future
complications.
Time to presentation
Tetanus status
Update with tetanus vaccination if indicated. If the patient is obtunded or unsure, tetanus
prophylaxis should be initiated.
Physical Examination
Clinical evaluation
Initial assessment begins with an evaluation of airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and
exposure.
A thorough physical examination should include circumferential evaluation of all limbs. Open
fractures may be missed in difficult-to-access regions that are not readily visible with the
patient in the supine position.

Physical Examination
Approximately one third of patients with an open fracture have associated injuries;
therefore, life-threatening injuries must be assessed, and treatment must begin
immediately. The treating physician should not let the presence of an open fracture
distract from associated injuries to the head, chest, abdomen, pelvis, and spine.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Open Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004090
5/21

All four extremities must be assessed for injury and, if possible, a detailed neurovascular
examination must be performed. A complete soft-tissue assessment, palpation for
tenderness, and observation of any deformity also are included in the initial evaluation.
Neurovascular Examination

Neurovascular Examination
Open fractures may be associated with vascular or neurologic damage. Vascular status
should be assessed via palpation or Doppler ultrasonography. If asymmetric lower
extremity pulses are present, ankle-brachial index should be performed. A thorough
neurologic examination is critical.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
In any patient in whom an open fracture is suspected, AP and lateral radiographs of the
affected area should be obtained in addition to radiographs that include the joints above and
below the location of the fracture. These radiographs should be obtained as soon as possible
to allow for preoperative planning.
Computed Tomography
CT is ordered if clinically indicated. In patients with a periarticular fracture in whom temporary
spanning external fixation is planned, CT often is best delayed until after the joint has been
spanned to improve understanding of the fracture details.
Other Studies
Angiography and a vascular consultation are performed based on clinical suspicion of vascular
injury, the type of injury, and the following indications.
SEND FEEDBACK

Knee dislocation or equivalent (eg, medial tibial plateau fracture) with ankle-brachial index less
than 0.9
Cool, pale foot with poor distal capillary refill
High-energy injury in an area of compromise (eg, trifurcation of the popliteal artery)
Any lower extremity injury with documented ankle-brachial index less than 0.9
Differential Diagnosis
Compartment syndrome must be considered a possibility in all patients with an extremity
fracture, even open fractures.
Management
Preoperative Stabilization
Indications
All patients with an open fracture should be treated with antibiotic agents and have their
tetanus updated (if uncertain or required) on presentation.
Emergency Department Care
Tetanus prophylaxis should be administered if appropriate (Table 3), and antibiotic
prophylaxis should begin immediately to reduce the risk of infection in patients with an open
fracture.1
Bleeding should be controlled via direct pressure rather than with the use of limb tourniquets
or blind clamping.
Manual exploration of the wound in the emergency department is not indicated if formal
surgical management is planned. Exploration in the emergency department risks additional
contamination and hemorrhage and neurovascular injury.
The open wound can be covered with the use of saline-moistened gauze, and the extremity
can be splinted. Effort should be made to reduce the bony fragments beneath the soft tissues
if possible to avoid additional soft-tissue pressure injury.2

Nonsurgical Management
Tetanus prophylaxis: two methods available (Table 1)
The dose of toxoid is 0.5 mL.
The dose for immune globulin is 75 U for patients younger than 5 years, 125 U for patients
aged 5 to 10 years, and 250 U for patients older than 10 years.
Both are administered intramuscularly into different sites and from different syringes.
Intravenous antibiotic agents
Antibiotic agents should be administered immediately on arrival in the emergency
department. Lack et al1 showed that antibiotic administration more than 66 minutes
postinjury was independently associated with an increased risk of infection.
In open fractures, gram-positive bacteria are the most common infecting organisms, with
gram-negative infections typically occurring half as frequently.
Data to indicate the optimal antibiotic treatment and duration of treatment in patients with
an open fracture are lacking.
Antibiotic therapy should include a first-generation cephalosporin (gram-positive coverage).
Aminoglycosides are used variably for expanded gram-negative coverage because of the
lower incidence of gram-negative infections and the risk of adverse medication effects (acute
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Open Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004090
8/21

renal failure, ototoxicity). Clindamycin is an effective alternative to a first-generation
cephalosporin.
If anaerobic infection is a substantial risk (eg, vascular injury, farm injury), ampicillin or
penicillin should be added to the antibiotic regimen. For freshwater or saltwater wounds, a
fluoroquinolone typically is added.
Antibiotic therapy is recommended for 24 to 72 hours after each débridement.
Local antibiotic therapy (whether topical antibiotic powder or in the form of antibiotic
impregnated polymethyl methacrylate) is a useful adjunct to systemic antibiotic therapy in
the management of open fractures at high risk for infection.
Nonsurgical Fracture Management
Stable fractures may occur and still be open fractures; this commonly occurs in patients with
an out-to-in open fracture pattern. In these patients, management of the fracture may include
irrigation and débridement without formal fracture fixation if the fracture is mechanically
stable and does not require fixation to maintain alignment and to support the soft tissues.
Surgical Management
Indications
Limb Salvage Versus Amputation
Indications for immediate or early amputation
Nonviable limb, irreparable vascular injury, warm ischemia time greater than 8 hours, or a
severe crush injury with minimal remaining viable tissue
Anticipated function after limb salvage will be less than that expected after amputation and
prosthetic application
The patient has medical comorbidities such that limb salvage will constitute a threat to the
patient’s life (eg, severe crush injury in a patient with chronic kidney disease)
The patient sustained severe multiple trauma such that limb salvage may be life threatening;
attempted salvage of a marginal extremity may result in a high metabolic cost or a large
necrotic/inflammatory load that may precipitate pulmonary or multiple organ failure.
Limb salvage is incompatible with the personal, sociologic, and economic consequences the
patient is willing to withstand because of the demand of multiple surgical procedures and
prolonged reconstruction time
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Open Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004090
9/21

The indications for limb salvage versus amputation are controversial and must account for
patient medical and social factors and injury features.
The Lower Extremity Assessment Project was a prospective, multicenter, observational study
of patients with a severe open lower extremity injury. Functional outcomes at 2 and 7 years
were similar between patients who underwent amputation versus limb salvage. Patients who
underwent limb salvage underwent more surgical procedures and were more likely to be re-
hospitalized for a major complication.2
Débridement
Thorough débridement is the most important aspect of early management of open fractures
in reducing the risk for early and late infection.
The timing of débridement is controversial; however, formal débridement in the operating
room is indicated unless the patient is clinically too unstable to go to the operating room.
Contraindications
The patient is too unstable for any surgical treatment
If this is the case, the patient should be taken for débridement at the earliest possible time,
after clinically able.
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Surgical timing—Contaminated surfaces permit bacterial adherence, and glycocalyx formation
occurs within approximately 6 hours postinjury. Although this results in enhanced protection
of bacteria, no clear evidence exists to support the optimal timing of surgical débridement of
an open fracture. If severe contamination is not present, several recent clinical studies have
shown no difference in infection rate between surgical débridement that occurred within 6
hours postinjury and surgical débridement that occurred 6 to 24 hours postinjury.3-5
Surgical Techniques
The wound should be extended proximally and distally to expose and facilitate exploration
and thorough débridement of the entire zone of injury.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Open Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004090
10/21

Intraoperative culture is not indicated acutely in patients with an open fracture because the
organisms isolated from an initial culture typically are not the bacteria that ultimately result in
infection.
All clearly devitalized soft tissue should be débrided, including skin, muscle, and bone, and any
gross contaminants should be removed.
Subsequent débridement may be necessary for severely contaminated wounds or for crush
injuries because tissues continue to declare their viability over a period of several days.
Volume and method of irrigation
Little research has reported an ideal volume that should be used for open fractures. A
common recommendation is 3 L for type I open fractures, 6 L for type II open fractures, and
9 L for type III open fractures.
Recent results from a prospective, multicenter randomized trial found similar revision
surgery rates regardless of irrigation pressure—high pressure, more than 20 psi; low
pressure, 5 to 10 psi; and very low pressure, 1 to 2 psi6 (Resource 1).
Contents of irrigation
Current recommendation: normal saline
Fracture stabilization (Figure 1)
Stabilization allows for better patient mobility, helps prevent additional damage to the
surrounding soft tissues, and makes overall treatment of the patient more manageable.
The type of fracture stabilization (ie, internal or external fixation) depends on the fracture
location and the degree of soft-tissue injury (Figure 2; Video 1).

Local antibiotic administration
New research is focusing on the use of local antibiotic agents in the forms of powder or bead
pouches after open fracture (Figure 3).
Early evidence suggests that the use of local antibiotic agents may decrease infection rates
after high-risk open fracture without increasing systemic adverse effects, such as renal
failure (Resource 2).

9/3/26, 5:25 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004090

Figure 3 Clinical photograph of an ankle shows antibiotic beads, which aer used to help prevent
infection during temporary wound coverage. (Reproduced from Zalavras CG, Marcus RE, Levin LS,
Patzakis MJ: Management of open fractures and subsequent complications. Instr Course Lect
2008;57:51-63.)
Soft-tissue coverage
Planning for soft-tissue closure should begin at the time of initial débridement.
Options for wound coverage before definitive closure include negative pressure wound
therapy (NPWT), antibiotic bead pouches, and wet-to-dry dressings. Wounds in patients with
an open fracture managed via NPWT are associated with a lower infection rate than those
managed via wet-to-dry dressings. Antibiotic bead pouches typically are used in patients with
severe contamination, if repeat débridement is planned, or for dead space management.
Immediate closure is preferred if the surgeon has determined that adequate débridement
has been performed, tension-free closure can be attained, no farmyard or fecal
contamination is present, and vascularity to the affected area is good. Most open fracture
wounds may be safely closed primarily after thorough surgical débridement.
Flap coverage, if required, should be performed as early as possible to minimize the risk of
infection. Recent data suggest that the risk of complications and/or infection increases if soft-
tissue coverage occurs more than 5 to 7 days postinjury. Lack et al1 reported an infection

rate of 5.4% in type III open tibia fractures covered within 5 days postinjury compared with
31.7% in those covered more than 5 days postinjury. Similarly, D’Alleyrand et al7 reported an
increase in the risk for complications (11%) and of infection (16%) for each additional day of
delay in soft-tissue coverage beyond day seven postinjury, whereas no increased risk was
observed if coverage occurred within 7 days postinjury (Video 2).
Video 2 Levin LS: Comprehensive management of soft tissue infections: New treatment
modalities, from Patzakis MJ, mod: Open fractures: Principles of management. Presented at the
Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16,
2019.
Bone grafting/adjuncts
These procedures are performed if the wound is clean, closed, and dry.
The timing of bone grafting is controversial. Some studies advocate grafting at the time of
definitive coverage; other studies advocate waiting a period of time (typically 6 weeks) after
definitive closure.8 If delayed grafting is to be performed, an antibiotic spacer commonly is
placed within the defect. The capsule that forms around the spacer has been shown to result
in the highest level of growth factors present at 6 weeks, making this an ideal time to
perform bone grafting if required.


Techniques/Procedures
In a prospective, multicenter randomized trial, a higher revision surgery rate was
reported for patients with an open fracture irrigated with the use of a soap solution
compared with patients with an open fracture irrigated the use of with normal saline
(Resource 1).
In a prospective randomized study, no substantial difference was noted in bone healing
or infection rates if a soap solution was used compared with a bacitracin solution.9
Wound healing problems were more common in the bacitracin group.
Negative Pressure Wound Therapy
NPWT works by promoting local wound perfusion.
The use of NPWT in the management of open fractures is controversial. Evidence supports and
refutes the use of NPWT, and cost-effectiveness remains uncertain.

Negative Pressure Wound Therapy
A multicenter prospective study published by Tahir et al6 reported insufficient evidence
to recommend the NPWT device over a standard gauze dressing for open fracture soft-
tissue defects. Iheozor-Ejiofor et al10 concluded with moderate certainty that no
difference exists between NPWT and standard therapy (Resources 3 and 4).
Other studies have reported a decreased infection rate and healthier granulation tissue
beds and a lower risk of flap failure in high-risk wounds associated with tibia fractures11
(Resource 5).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Open Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004090
17/21

The benefit of NPWT is still being investigated. Although evidence suggests that NPWT
may not be cost-effective for all open fracture wounds, it may be beneficial for some
high-risk wounds after open fracture.
Postoperative Management
Severe or contaminated wounds may require repeat irrigation and débridement until a
healthy, clean wound environment exists for definitive fixation and soft-tissue coverage.
Complications
Risk of infection after open fracture is higher than after closed fracture, and risk increases
from approximately 1% in type I open fractures to 30% or higher in type III open fractures.
Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation begins as soon as possible and is based on fracture pattern and the
characteristics of the injury and soft tissues.
Outcomes
Infection risk after open fractures depends on the severity of the injury (Tables 2 and 3).
The number of medical and immunocompromising comorbidities (eg, age older than 80 years,
nicotine use, diabetes mellitus, malignancy, pulmonary insufficiency, systemic
immunodeficiency) has been shown to be a substantial predictor of infection in patients with
an open fracture of the long bones: class A (no comorbidities), 4%; class B (one or two
comorbidities), 15%; and class C (three or more comorbidities), 31%.
Pearls and Pitfalls
Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for open fracture.
Appropriate antibiotic agents should be administered as soon as possible, within 1 hour of
arrival to the emergency department.
The Gustilo-Anderson classification system is used after initial débridement.
Copious low-flow saline is a reasonable, low-cost method for the irrigation of open fractures.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:25 PM
AAOS | Open Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004090
18/21

Débridement should be thorough, and all clearly devitalized and contaminated tissue should
be removed.
Local antibiotic administration is an area of ongoing research; however, early results are
promising.
Clinicians should consider temporary or definitive fracture fixation at the time of débridement
to protect the surrounding soft tissues.
NPWT is controversial but may be indicated in patients with a high-risk wound.
Evidence suggests that routine use of NPWT is not cost-effective.
